title: Promote and maintain professionalism in extension

lessons.title: What professionalism means in extension
lessons.html:
Extension as a profession

Extension practitioners hold a position of trust. Farmers act on their advice, sometimes risking a season's crop or a herd's health. Professionalism means consistently applying sound knowledge, ethical behaviour and reliable service.

Elements of professionalism

  • Competence - technical knowledge of crops, livestock, soils and markets, plus facilitation and communication skills.
  • Integrity - honesty, keeping promises and admitting mistakes.
  • Accountability - taking responsibility for your advice and reporting accurately.
  • Respect - for farmers of all backgrounds, languages, genders and farm sizes.
  • Reliability - arriving on time, following up, answering calls.
  • Confidentiality - protecting farmers' financial and personal information.

Professional registration

In South Africa, extension and advisory practitioners may register with the South African Council for Natural Scientific Professions (SACNASP) in an agricultural field, and many belong to the South African Society for Agricultural Extension (SASAE). Registration and membership signal commitment to a code of conduct and to continuing professional development. Check the current requirements with these bodies directly.

Why professionalism matters

Past failures in some development projects damaged farmers' trust in officials. A professional practitioner rebuilds that trust through consistent, honest service. Professionalism also protects the practitioner: accurate records and evidence-based advice are the best defence if advice is questioned.

Recognising unprofessional conduct

  • Promising support that has not been approved.
  • Favouring relatives or friends when allocating inputs.
  • Recommending products because a supplier offers personal benefits.
  • Missing appointments without notice.
  • Giving advice outside your competence instead of referring.

lessons.title: Ethics and conflicts of interest
lessons.html:
Making ethical decisions

Ethics deals with what is right and fair. Extension practitioners face real dilemmas, for example being offered a lamb as a thank-you gift, or being asked by a councillor to prioritise certain households for a support programme.

Conflicts of interest

A conflict of interest occurs when personal interests could influence professional decisions. Examples:

  • Owning a farm supply business while advising farmers what to buy.
  • Being related to a member of a project that you are assessing for funding.
  • Accepting gifts or hospitality from a supplier whose product you recommend.

Declare any possible conflict to your supervisor in writing and step back from the decision. Follow your employer's policy on gifts; public servants are bound by the public service code of conduct and must declare interests as required.

A simple ethical decision process

  1. Identify the issue and who is affected.
  2. Check the law, policies and code of conduct.
  3. Consider the options and their consequences for farmers, the employer and yourself.
  4. Ask: would I be comfortable if this decision were reported in the local newspaper?
  5. Consult a supervisor or colleague when unsure.
  6. Decide, act and record the reasons.

Fairness and inclusion

Allocate time and resources fairly, using clear criteria. Make sure women farmers, young people and farm workers are not overlooked. Treat a smallholder with five goats with the same respect as a commercial farmer with 500 cattle.

Evidence-based advice

Base recommendations on research, registered products and proven practice. For agricultural remedies, only recommend products registered under Act 36 of 1947 and tell farmers to follow the label. When you do not know, say so and find out, or refer the farmer to a specialist such as a state vet or soil scientist.

lessons.title: Maintaining professionalism over a career
lessons.html:
Keeping standards high

Professionalism is not achieved once; it is maintained over a career and promoted among colleagues.

Continuing professional development (CPD)

  • Attend short courses, symposia and farmers' days.
  • Read research summaries from the Agricultural Research Council, universities and commodity organisations.
  • Learn from farmers and from colleagues through study tours and peer learning.
  • Keep a CPD record of activities and what you learnt.

Self-management

  • Plan your week, prioritise farmer needs and keep a diary.
  • Keep accurate visit reports and records.
  • Manage stress and workload; rural extension involves long distances and pressure.
  • Look after official vehicles and equipment, and follow road safety rules.

Safety and wellbeing on farm visits

Follow your employer's safety rules under the OHS Act 85 of 1993: wear suitable footwear and protective clothing, keep a safe distance from handling facilities when animals are being worked, never enter an area where spraying is taking place, and let the office know your route.

Promoting professionalism in others

  • Model good behaviour: punctuality, respect and honesty.
  • Mentor new practitioners and share materials.
  • Give constructive feedback to colleagues privately and respectfully.
  • Report serious misconduct, such as fraud, through the proper channels.
  • Take part in professional associations and contribute to discussions about extension policy.

Reflective practice

After important activities, ask: What went well? What could I do better? What will I change next time? Regular reflection builds skill and humility.

Key points

  • Professionalism combines competence, integrity, accountability, respect, reliability and confidentiality.
  • Declare conflicts of interest and follow gift policies.
  • Give evidence-based advice and refer when outside your competence.
  • Keep up CPD and accurate records.
  • Promote professionalism by example, mentoring and reporting misconduct.
